title: Loops: Repeat Forever, Repeat N Times
description: The third and final shape. Say a step once, ask for it to happen many times — and watch a long sequence collapse into a handful of blocks.

content.value: A loop runs the blocks inside it more than once. This course's block palette has two versions: repeat N times, which runs a fixed number of times and then stops, and repeat forever, which keeps going with no built-in end — useful, but genuinely dangerous if nothing inside it ever changes the situation.

content.title: 🧩 Solve it with a loop
content.hint: This maze repeats a pattern. Try wrapping 'forward, forward, right' in a Repeat block instead of stacking it out by hand.

content.value: Notice you can solve that maze two ways: stack out every single forward and turn by hand, or wrap the repeating pattern in one Repeat block. Both reach the flag — but the loop version is shorter, and more importantly, it's shorter in a way that reveals the pattern in the maze itself. That's usually a sign a loop is the right tool.

A repeat forever block never exits on its own — it only stops if something inside it, like a decision, breaks the pattern (for example, stopping once the flag is reached). Without that, it would run endlessly. The maze widget protects you with a safety limit so a runaway loop can't actually freeze anything, but a real robot has no such guardrail unless you build one in yourself.
Real code has the exact same two shapes, just written differently: `for i in range(n):` is repeat N times, and `while True:` is repeat forever. You'll meet both by name in the next module.

Key takeaway: a loop repeats its contents — either a fixed number of times, or forever until something inside it stops the pattern. Spotting a repeating pattern and replacing it with a loop is one of the most useful moves in programming.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between 'repeat 3 times' and 'repeat forever'?
options: 'Repeat 3 times' stops on its own after 3 runs; 'repeat forever' has no built-in end
quiz.explain: A fixed-count loop is self-limiting. An unlimited loop keeps going unless something inside it (like a decision) breaks the pattern.

quiz.question: A maze needs 'forward, forward, right' repeated four times. What's the advantage of wrapping that in a loop instead of writing all twelve blocks by hand?
options: No real advantage, both work identically well
It's shorter and makes the repeating pattern in the maze visible in the program itself
Loops always run faster in real time
quiz.explain: Both solve the maze, but the loop version is more concise and honestly reflects the structure of the problem — which is exactly why it earns more stars.

quiz.question: What's the risk of a 'repeat forever' block with nothing inside it that can change the situation?
options: It runs endlessly, with no way to stop on its own
It's exactly as safe as a fixed-count loop
quiz.explain: Without a condition or decision that can break the pattern, an unlimited loop truly never ends on its own — a real risk to design around.
